issues.legal_issue: A judgment cannot remain in force when it conflicts with a later ruling of a larger bench on the same issue.
material_facts: Different benches of equal strength had reached conflicting conclusions about the pricing of flats under the same scheme.
A Full Bench later upheld the revised pricing and rejected the challenge to it.
The appeals concerned an earlier judgment that had reached the opposite conclusion, and the challenge to the Full Bench ruling had been dismissed.
issues.conclusion: The conflicting judgment was set aside, and the writ petitions were disposed of in accordance with the Full Bench ruling.
issues.legal_principle: A larger bench resolves a conflict between decisions of benches of equal strength. Contradictory rulings on the same point should not be allowed to operate simultaneously; consistency and certainty require the conflicting judgment to yield to the larger-bench ruling.

predicates.appeal_against_conflicting_judgment: A party appealed from a judgment that decided an issue also addressed by a larger bench.
predicates.later_larger_bench_decided_same_issue: A larger bench later decided the same issue.
predicates.larger_bench_ruling_conflicts: The larger bench reached a conclusion inconsistent with the judgment under appeal.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges a judgment that conflicts with a later ruling of a larger bench on the same issue, the conflicting judgment is set aside and the proceeding is disposed of under the larger-bench ruling.

issues.legal_issue: A public authority’s revised pricing under a contractual allotment scheme is not subject to interference where the stated prices are indicative and the authority explains the basis for the revision.
material_facts: The scheme brochure described the estimated prices as illustrative and subject to revision or modification, including for changes in construction costs and other exigencies.
The authority revised the land rates used to calculate flat prices after considering relevant factors.
The authority placed material before the Full Bench explaining how the prices had been calculated and why the land rates had increased.
The Full Bench found the revised rates neither arbitrary nor illegal.
issues.conclusion: The Court agreed with the Full Bench that the revised pricing was neither arbitrary nor illegal and that the High Court should not have interfered with it under Article 226.
issues.legal_principle: Clauses 13 and 14 of the scheme brochure made the stated prices illustrative and subject to revision, and the allotment transaction was contractual; in those circumstances, the Full Bench held that Article 226 did not permit interference with the costing, including escalation in land cost. The respondents relied on Bareilly Development Authority v. Ajai Pal Singh, but the judgment explains that the relevant pricing material was placed before the Full Bench, unlike the asserted failure to explain pricing in the earlier proceedings.

rule.if: writ_challenge_to_scheme_pricing and contractual_allotment_scheme and stated_prices_revisable and authority_explained_revision_basis

predicates.writ_challenge_to_scheme_pricing: A party brought a writ proceeding challenging prices charged under an allotment scheme.
predicates.contractual_allotment_scheme: The allotment arose from a contractual scheme between the authority and registrants.
predicates.stated_prices_revisable: The scheme stated that its estimated prices were illustrative and could be revised.
predicates.authority_explained_revision_basis: The authority provided material explaining the basis for its revised pricing.

issues.definition: A pricing revision is not interfered with when a writ challenge concerns a contractual allotment scheme whose stated prices are revisable and the authority explains the basis for the revision.
